name: Reactive Oxygen Species Generation, Antioxidant Defense Systems, and Reperfusion Injury

reference.source: Medical Biochemistry 5th ed / Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32nd ed
clinicalPearls: Superoxide is converted by superoxide dismutase into H2O2; ferrous iron catalyzes the Fenton reaction generating toxic OH.
Catalase in peroxisomes and glutathione peroxidase in cytosol/mitochondria reduce hydrogen peroxide to water
Glutathione reductase regenerates reduced glutathione (GSH) using NADPH supplied by the G6PD-driven HMP shunt
Phagocytic NADPH oxidase generates the respiratory burst; its genetic deficiency causes Chronic Granulomatous Disease
Reperfusion restores oxygen to ischemic tissue where xanthine oxidase metabolizes hypoxanthine, unleasing destructive ROS
reference.pathophysiology: Mitochondrial electron transport and inflammatory enzymes generate reactive oxygen species. In phagosomes, NADPH oxidase generates superoxide, converted to hypochlorous acid by myeloperoxidase. In Chronic Granulomatous Disease, defective NADPH oxidase prevents ROS generation, impairing killing of catalase-positive microbes. During reperfusion, hypoxanthine accumulated during ischemia is rapidly oxidized by xanthine oxidase, unleasing massive superoxide that peroxidizes sarcolemmal lipids.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (recurrent Staphylococcus, Aspergillus infections)
G6PD deficiency (oxidative stress-induced hemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells)
additionalInvestigations: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry or Nitroblue Tetrazolium (NBT) reduction test for CGD
G6PD quantitative enzymatic activity assay (measured outside of acute hemolytic crisis)
Serum malondialdehyde or F2-isoprostanes as biomarkers of lipid peroxidation
Myeloperoxidase (MPO) staining on peripheral blood or bone marrow smears
